original_question: What can be proved about the three virtual-link crossing numbers C, V, and T, about the classical and virtual unknotting numbers, about the relationship between the minimal number of virtual crossings and the least genus of a surface realization, about whether T = V + L, about algorithms for finding V in some classes, and about nontrivial upper and lower bounds for T, V, and L coming from virtual knot polynomials?
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the paper’s crossing-number open problem: it names the three crossing invariants C, V, and T; mentions the classical and virtual unknotting notions introduced there; asks about the relation between minimal virtual crossings and minimal supporting genus; includes the equality question for T versus the other crossing counts; asks about algorithms for computing V in special classes; and asks for polynomial upper/lower bounds. These are exactly the components grouped together in Section 7, Problem 16.
missing_details: The problem is explicitly stated for each virtual link L, and C, V, T are functions of L: C(L) is the minimum number of classical crossings, V(L) the minimum number of virtual crossings, and T(L) the minimum total number of crossings, each minimized over all virtual-diagram representatives of L.
The unknotting-number part is stated for knots, not general links: the classical unknotting number counts crossing switches needed to unknot the knot, minimized over all diagrams of that knot.
The virtual unknotting number is the minimum number of crossings that must be changed from classical to virtual by direct flattening, minimized over all virtual diagrams of the knot.

To be paper-faithful, one should distinguish direct flattening from the earlier operation of crossing virtualization in the paper, where a classical crossing is replaced by a crossing flanked by two virtual crossings; Problem 16 uses direct flattening, not that earlier virtualization move.

The genus question concerns the least genus of a surface realization in the paper’s thickened-surface/stable-equivalence model of virtual links, i.e. embeddings in thickened surfaces considered up to isotopy, surface homeomorphism, and addition/removal of empty handles.

The nearby context adds an important hidden fact: the minimal embedding genus can be strictly smaller than the number of virtual crossings in a diagram, which is why the genus-versus-V question is nontrivial.

The statement "Is it true that T = V + L?" is not stand-alone as written, because L already denotes the link rather than a numerical invariant; in context this is almost certainly a typographical slip and needs clarification in any refined version.
Likewise, the phrase "upper and lower bounds for T, V, L" should be clarified to bounds for the crossing-number invariants, almost certainly C, V, and T.
The algorithmic part is narrowly phrased: the paper asks for an algorithm for finding V for some class of virtual knots; it only notes that T is partially understood in certain cited cases.

The official problem says very little is known and specifically asks to "find out more about the virtual unknotting number"; a stand-alone reformulation should preserve that this is the unknotting subproblem the paper emphasizes.
refined_question: For each virtual link L, let C(L), V(L), and T(L) denote, respectively, the minima over all virtual-diagram representatives of L of the numbers of classical crossings, virtual crossings, and total crossings. For a virtual knot K, let u_cl(K) be the minimum number of crossing switches needed to unknot K, taken over all diagrams of K, and let u_v(K) be the minimum number of direct flattenings (changing a classical crossing into a virtual crossing) needed to unknot K, taken over all virtual diagrams of K. Determine the basic relations and effective estimates for these invariants: in particular, develop the theory of the virtual unknotting number u_v(K); relate V(K) to the least genus among stable surface realizations of K; decide whether T(L)=C(L)+V(L) (the paper prints "T=V+L"); find algorithms for computing V(L) in some classes of virtual knots/links; and obtain nontrivial upper and lower bounds for C(L), V(L), and T(L) from virtual-knot polynomials.
justification: The draft matches Section 7, Problem 16 on p. 25 essentially line by line, so that is the nearest official formulation. To make the question stand-alone, one needs the paper’s definitions of virtual links as stable classes of embeddings in thickened surfaces (§2.2, p. 5), the distinction between direct flattening and the earlier virtualization move (§2, pp. 8-9), and the nearby remark that minimal embedding genus can be strictly less than the number of virtual crossings in a diagram (§2, p. 10). The printed formulas "T = V + L" and "bounds for T, V, L" are inconsistent with the immediately preceding definitions of C, V, T in Problem 16, so clarifying them is necessary; the natural paper-faithful repair is that the intended numerical relation is with C, not with the link symbol L.
